content.title: About
content.content: Cheese is a dairy product made by coagulating milk and pressing the curds. In sandwiches a wide range of cheeses is used – soft (mozzarella, brie), semi‑hard (cheddar, gouda) and hard (parmesan, emmental). Cheese adds creaminess, rich flavor and boosts the nutritional value of a sandwich.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese has been produced for more than 7,000 years; the earliest archaeological evidence dates to 5,000 BC.
There are over 1,800 recognized cheese varieties worldwide, each with distinct taste and texture.
Cheese often acts as the “glue” in sandwiches, binding ingredients together.
Hard cheeses like parmesan can be grated onto bread, creating a crunchy crust.
Pre‑sliced cheese strips are popular for quick sandwich assembly.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese is one of the best dietary sources of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Provides high‑quality protein
items.content: Cheese supplies complete animal protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese contains riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: Certain cheeses, especially those from whole milk, contain conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) that may support metabolism.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermented cheeses such as camembert and brie contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating soft and semi‑hard cheeses.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses are salty; individuals with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause severe reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Hard cheeses are calorie‑dense and high in saturated fat, so portion size should be moderated.

items.title: Biogenic amines
items.content: Aged cheeses may contain histamine and tyramine, which can trigger headaches in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese can be sliced thin, grated, or melted. In sandwiches it serves as a base (cheddar in a classic cheeseburger), a complement to vegetables (mozzarella with tomato), or a flavorful topping (parmesan on an Italian panini).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Hard cheeses keep for several months, soft cheeses up to a week. Before use, check for off‑odors or unusual mold; discard if present.
